summary: Defines a way for SDP offer/answer endpoints to negotiate which Quality of Service mechanism to use for a media stream, since several are available on the Internet. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Two people setting up a call must agree on how to reserve speed for it, since there is more than one way. This gives them a way to talk about it.

questions: how to negotiate qos mechanism in sdp
how do endpoints negotiate qos mechanism
what are rsvp and nsis tokens in sdp
subtitle: Two SDP attributes that let endpoints agree on which QoS mechanism, such as RSVP or NSIS, to use for a media stream.

tldr.problem: The SDP offer/answer model assumes endpoints somehow establish the QoS they need, but on the Internet more than one QoS mechanism is available and there was no way to negotiate which one to use.
tldr.mechanism: The offerer lists the QoS mechanisms it supports for sending and for receiving, in order of preference, in the qos-mech-send and qos-mech-recv attributes. The answerer returns the ones it also supports.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints get an ordered list of common mechanisms per direction and try them in priority order. Whether the network actually supports a mechanism is outside the document.

today: RFC 5432 is a Proposed Standard, and no obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it.

sections.title: The Problem and Its Limits
sections.content:
The offer/answer model (RFC 3264) for SDP (RFC 4566) gives endpoints no way to negotiate the Quality of Service (QoS) mechanism for a media stream. Even with QoS preconditions (RFC 3312), the choice of mechanism is left to the endpoints. Endpoints in closed environments typically agree out of band, but on the Internet more than one QoS service is available.

Examples of QoS mechanisms are RSVP (RFC 2205) and NSIS. The RFC is clear about its limits: agreeing on a mechanism does not mean the network supports it, and discovering what the network supports is out of scope. The exchanged information can still help a network operator choose a mechanism acceptable to both endpoints and debug misconfiguration.
sections.eli5: There is more than one way to reserve a fast lane for a call. Before this, the two callers had no standard way to say which way they know how to use.

sections.title: The Two SDP Attributes
sections.content:
The document defines qos-mech-send and qos-mech-recv, both usable at the session and media level. Each holds a list of qos-mech tokens: rsvp, nsis or an extension token.

A token in qos-mech-send names a mechanism that can reserve resources for traffic sent by the entity that generated the session description. A token in qos-mech-recv does the same for traffic it receives. The two attributes are not interdependent, so one can be used without the other.

The RFC's example media line is m=audio 50000 RTP/AVP 0 followed by a=qos-mech-send: rsvp nsis and a=qos-mech-recv: rsvp nsis.
sections.eli5: There are two little labels. One says how I can reserve the lane for what I send, and the other says how I can reserve the lane for what I receive.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Behavior
sections.content:
The offerer puts in each attribute the mechanisms it supports for that direction, in order of preference. The answerer mirrors the directions: tokens from the offer's qos-mech-send that it supports in the receive direction go into its qos-mech-recv, and tokens from the offer's qos-mech-recv that it supports for sending go into its qos-mech-send. It may order the tokens by its own preferences and the offer's, but the ordering algorithm is out of scope. If nothing is in common, it returns empty attributes.

Which direction needs QoS is negotiated by other means, such as preconditions, and so are mechanism parameters like the bandwidth to reserve.

After the exchange, both sides use the answer's lists. They SHOULD try the highest-priority mechanism in each direction first, then the next one, and so on. If all common mechanisms fail, an endpoint MAY try mechanisms the other side does not support, because a network entity out of its control, such as an RSVP proxy, may make them work.

If a later offer in an established session lacks the attribute for a direction, the endpoints SHOULD keep using the mechanism already in use.
sections.eli5: One side shows its list of tricks in order of favorite. The other side crosses out the ones it cannot do and sends the list back. Then both try the top trick first, and the next one if that fails.

sections.title: Example Exchange
sections.content: The offerer lists both RSVP and NSIS for both directions and puts RSVP first, because it prefers it. The answerer supports NSIS in both directions but not RSVP, so its answer lists only nsis in qos-mech-send and qos-mech-recv. The endpoints therefore use NSIS.
sections.eli5: I say I can do trick A or trick B and I like A more. You can only do B, so you answer with B, and we both use B.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the two attributes under the SDP Parameters registry, both at session and media level and not subject to charset. It also created a subregistry of QoS mechanism tokens with initial values rsvp and nsis, both referencing RFC 5432. New tokens follow the 'Specification Required' policy from RFC 5226.
sections.eli5: A public list was started that holds the names of the allowed tricks. New names can be added only when someone writes down how the trick works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker may add, modify or remove the qos-mech-send and qos-mech-recv attributes in a session description. The endpoints might then be unable to find a common QoS mechanism, and the application could behave badly.

The RFC therefore strongly RECOMMENDS integrity and authenticity protection of SDP carrying these attributes. For SDP carried in SIP (RFC 3261), S/MIME is the natural choice for end-to-end integrity protection. Other applications MAY use a different form of integrity protection.
sections.eli5: If a sneaky person scribbles on the list while it travels, the two callers might think they have no trick in common. Sealing the message stops that.
